The split puts alternate nodes on opposite sides: A, C, E on side S (teal) and B, D, F on side T (violet). Every one of the six edges then runs between the two sides, so all six are cut edges in the accent color. The card gives the cut value 6.0 and the two sides." width="100%"} The maximum cut problem asks for a split of the nodes into two groups that maximizes the number (or total weight) of edges with one end in each group. It models choosing opposing teams or sides so that conflicts (edges) fall between them, assigning components to two circuit layers to minimize same-layer connections, and it is a standard benchmark for optimization. Max-cut is NP-hard, so these methods are heuristics: - `"one_exchange"` (default): local search that moves one node to the other side whenever that increases the cut, until no single move helps. The result cuts at least half of the total edge weight (with non-negative weights). - `"randomized"`: put each node on side `S` with probability `p`. With `p=0.5`, half the weight is cut on average. Edge direction is ignored, and self-loops never count. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["one_exchange"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : `"one_exchange"` (default) or `"randomized"`. [initial]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : One-exchange only: nodes (IDs or labels) that start on side `S`. If `None` (default), all nodes start on side `T`. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed. One-exchange uses it to break ties between equally good moves. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.5]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Randomized only: the probability that a node is put on side `S`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[float, tuple[list[int], list[int]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The cut weight and the two sides `(S, T)` as lists of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `method=` is unknown, `p` is outside $[0, 1]$, or a node in `initial` does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} One-exchange keeps, for every node, the gain of moving it (the weight of its edges to its own side minus the weight to the other side) and repeatedly moves a node with the largest positive gain, updating its neighbors' gains in $O(\deg)$. At a local optimum every node has at least half of its incident weight crossing the cut, so the cut holds at least half the total weight. Each move strictly increases the cut, so the search terminates. This mirrors NetworkX's `one_exchange` and `randomized_partitioning`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a 6-cycle, putting alternate nodes on opposite sides cuts all 6 edges: ::: {#d9ebc24a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ring = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) ring.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "A")]) value, (S, T) = ring.maximum_cut(seed=1) value, sorted(ring.get_label_from_id(n) for n in S) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (6.0, ['A', 'C', 'E']) ``` ::: ::: A triangle can never be cut completely: one side always contains two of its nodes, so the best cut has 2 of the 3 edges: ::: {#7221fed9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tri = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) tri.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) tri.maximum_cut(seed=1)[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2.0 ``` ::: :::
